sections.text:
Tactile sensors are integral components of modern robotic systems, enabling robots to perceive and interact with the physical environment through tactile feedback. Despite their importance, the physical-layer security of tactile sensors has received little attention in prior work.

In this paper, we present GhostTac, to the best of our knowledge, the first contactless attack that manipulates tactile sensing via electromagnetic interference (EMI).

We identify that EMI exploits the nonlinear rectification and limited bandwidth amplification effects, allowing carefully crafted EMI signals to be converted into a persistent DC offset that bypasses on-board filtering and induces stable measurement deviations.

Building on this mechanism, GhostTac enables fine-grained and controllable manipulation of sensor outputs by reshaping the spatial distribution and manipulating the magnitude at the targeted location.

Such interference can induce unintended and harmful robot behaviors, such as causing a domestic robot to exert excessive force, resulting in physical damage or human injury. We evaluate GhostTac on 10 sensor modules and 2 dexterous hands, covering 15 tactile sensors of different types, and demonstrate consistent attack effectiveness across all tested devices.

We further present three case studies on tactile grasping, slip detection, and material classification to illustrate practical impacts in real robotic tasks. We envision that our findings shed light on a new physical attack vector against tactile sensing in robotic systems.

summary.en: The paper presents GhostTac, which the authors describe as the first contactless attack manipulating tactile sensing through electromagnetic interference (EMI). They attribute the effect to nonlinear rectification and limited-bandwidth amplification that convert crafted EMI into a persistent DC offset, bypass filtering, and create stable measurement deviations. Spatial and magnitude shaping enables targeted output manipulation. Evaluation covered 15 tactile sensors across 10 modules and two dexterous hands; the authors report effectiveness on all tested devices. Three case studies illustrate impacts on grasping, slip detection, and material classification.
summary.zh: 论文提出 GhostTac，作者称其为首个通过电磁干扰（EMI）无接触操纵触觉传感的攻击。其机制利用非线性整流和有限带宽放大，将精心设计的 EMI 信号转为持续直流偏移，绕过板载滤波并造成稳定测量偏差；通过改变空间分布和幅值，可定点操纵传感器输出。作者在10个传感器模块、2只灵巧手所覆盖的15种触觉传感器上评估，报告所有测试设备均受到有效攻击，并以抓取、滑移检测和材料分类三个案例说明可能影响。摘要指出，此类干扰可能诱发机器人过度施力等有害行为。

items.title: GhostTac: Manipulating Tactile Sensors without Physical Contact

sections.text:
This letter presents a trajectory planner for humanoid robots to perform dynamic motions on complex, parameterizable terrains using a contact-implicit whole-body optimization framework. The planner generates feasible movements without predefined contact sequences, considering the robot's full dynamics and kinematics.

To plan bipedal locomotion on steps, ramps, and other terrains, we propose a mathematical model to approximate ground geometry with a smooth surface. The rigid interaction between the robot and the ground is modeled via novel contact constraints, extending the domain of applicability from flat and horizontal surfaces to any arbitrary smooth surface.

Effectiveness is demonstrated using nonlinear programming to plan motions on various terrain topologies. We also explore dynamic trajectory generation by embedding high-level requirements in the cost function and the initial guess. Preliminary feasibility tests were conducted over non-coplanar terrains, both in simulation and on the real robot ErgoCub.

summary.en: The letter presents a contact-implicit whole-body trajectory optimizer for dynamic humanoid motion on parameterizable terrain. It generates feasible movements without predefined contact sequences and accounts for full-body dynamics and kinematics. Ground geometry is approximated by a smooth surface, with contact constraints intended to cover arbitrary smooth surfaces. Nonlinear programming demonstrations include steps, ramps, and other terrain topologies; the authors also explore embedding high-level requirements in the cost function and initial guess. Preliminary feasibility tests on non-coplanar terrain were conducted in simulation and on the ErgoCub robot.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种用于类人机器人动态运动规划的接触隐式全身轨迹优化方法，可在复杂、可参数化地形上生成动作，无需预先指定接触序列，并考虑机器人完整动力学与运动学。方法以平滑曲面近似地面几何，并用新的接触约束描述机器人与地面的刚性相互作用，扩展到任意光滑表面。作者通过非线性规划展示其在台阶、斜坡等地形上的规划效果，并探索将高层要求纳入代价函数和初始猜测来生成动态轨迹。初步可行性测试涵盖非共面地形，在仿真和 ErgoCub 实体机器人上进行。

sections.text:
A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields.

Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization.

On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture.

The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%.These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees.

Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only.

The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.

summary.en: The paper studies learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting semantic mismatches in robot action interfaces and ranking likely faulty fields. In a retrospective comparison on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks and 432 source episodes, the exact conditional of a joint mixture achieves higher recall than the joint mixture and a ridge residual at a fixed empirical clean false-positive rate. Joint scoring has slightly higher localization. The authors stress these results are not deployment calibration guarantees; evidence is bounded to offline diagnostics and a detection-localization tradeoff.
summary.zh: 本文研究利用学习到的状态—动作—效果关系作为离线契约，检测机器人动作接口中形状和范围正确、语义却不匹配的问题，并对可能出错的字段排序。在 LIBERO Spatial 十项任务、432 个源 episode 的回顾性比较中，固定经验干净误报率下，精确条件混合模型的召回率高于联合混合模型和岭回归残差；联合评分的定位率略高于条件评分。作者强调这些是回顾性诊断而非部署校准保证。其他基准、故障类型及修复或缓解测试多未通过相应门槛，因此证据仅支持有限的离线诊断能力及检测与定位间的权衡。

sections.text:
Rotation representations are foundational in fields such as computer graphics, robotics, and machine learning, where precise and efficient modeling of 3D orientations is critical.

This paper comprehensively investigates diverse representations of the special orthogonal group $SO（3）$, such as Euler angles, axis-angle vectors, quaternions, rotation matrices, exponential maps, and emerging continuous and probabilistic methods, evaluating their mathematical formulations, continuity, susceptibility to gimbal lock, computational efficiency, storage requirements, interpolation properties, and composition operations, while integrating detailed algebraic insights with practical applications in fields like animation, pose estimation, inertial navigation, 3D shape registration, and neural networks.

Empirical evidence highlights quaternions' dominance due to their compactness and computational efficiency, while alternatives like 6D continuous representations and matrix Fisher distributions provide enhanced continuity and uncertainty modeling.

Future research could explore hybrid methods and thorough large-scale evaluations to help build a solid foundation for improving rotation representation techniques.

summary.en: This paper compares representations of the 3D rotation group SO(3), including Euler angles, axis-angle vectors, quaternions, matrices, exponential maps, and continuous and probabilistic approaches. It discusses their mathematical formulations, continuity, gimbal-lock susceptibility, computational and storage costs, interpolation, composition, and applications. The authors report empirical evidence favoring quaternions for compactness and computational efficiency, while 6D continuous representations and matrix Fisher distributions offer advantages in continuity and uncertainty modeling. They suggest future work on hybrid methods and large-scale evaluations.

sections.text:
Low-cost four-degree-of-freedom (DoF) arms are among the most accessible robotic platforms.

But they are one joint short for picking up in situations where objects are at arbitrary orientations, a task that appears to require five degrees of freedom: the planar position (x and y), the height (z), a wrist rotation to align the gripper with the object, and gripper actuation, of which a four-DoF arm lacks the wrist rotation.

This work uses perception and motion planning so that such an arm, a roughly $200 Waveshare RoArm-M2-S under a fixed overhead camera, can detect and color-sort writing utensils without that joint.

A YOLO11n-OBB (You Only Look Once, oriented bounding box) detector locates each writing utensil; camera intrinsics and an ArUco reference pose convert its pixel coordinates to robot coordinates; and a color classifier labels it.

The detected orientation angle determines the motion strategy: utensils close to the arm's fixed approach direction are picked up directly, and those at steeper angles are reoriented via corrective sweeps until they are graspable, after which they are picked up and sorted into the assigned color bin.

In 196 single-utensil trials, the 98 that started beyond 45 degrees from that direction all became graspable within four sweeps (130 total).Overall, 176 (89.8%) ended in the correct bin; 19 of 20 failures were slipped or missed grasps, one a mislabeled color.

For the seven utensils tested in this setup, corrective sweeps brought every steeply misaligned utensil into a graspable orientation on an arm with no wrist joint.

summary.en: The paper presents a vision-guided method for detecting, reorienting, and color-sorting writing utensils with a low-cost four-degree-of-freedom arm and a fixed overhead camera. The system estimates utensil orientation and uses direct pickup or corrective sweeps before grasping. In 196 single-utensil trials, all 98 items initially more than 45 degrees from the fixed approach direction became graspable within four sweeps; 176 trials ended with placement in the correct color bin. The reported conclusion is limited to seven utensils tested in this setup.
summary.zh: 本文展示一种在固定俯视相机下，用低成本四自由度机械臂视觉识别并按颜色分拣书写工具的方法。系统检测工具方向，将像素位置转换为机器人坐标，并依据方向选择直接抓取或通过校正扫动重新定向。在 196 次单件试验中，98 件初始偏离固定接近方向超过 45 度的工具均在四次扫动内达到可抓取姿态；总体有 176 件进入正确颜色箱。作者报告的结论限于该设置中测试的七种工具。

sections.text:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning is a key method for training multi-robot systems. Through rewarding or punishing robots over a series of episodes according to their performance, they can be trained and then deployed in the real world. However, poorly trained policies can lead to unsafe behaviour during early training stages.

We introduce Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning guided by language-based Inter-robot Negotiation (MARLIN), a hybrid framework in which large language models provide high-level planning before the reinforcement learning policy has learned effective behaviours. Robots use language models to negotiate actions and generate plans that guide policy learning.

The system dynamically switches between reinforcement learning and language-model-based negotiation during training, enabling more effective exploration. MARLIN is evaluated using both simulated and physical robots with local and remote language models.

Results show that, compared to standard multi-agent reinforcement learning, the hybrid approach achieves higher performance in early training with limited impact on the final performance. The code is available at https://github.com/SooratiLab/MARLIN.

summary.en: The paper introduces MARLIN, a hybrid framework that uses language-model-based inter-robot negotiation to guide multi-agent reinforcement learning. Robots negotiate actions and produce plans to support policy learning before effective behaviors have been learned, with the system switching dynamically between negotiation and reinforcement learning during training. Evaluations use simulated and physical robots with local and remote language models. The authors report better performance than standard multi-agent reinforcement learning early in training, with limited impact on final performance.
summary.zh: 本文提出 MARLIN，一种以语言模型驱动机器人间协商来引导多智能体强化学习的混合框架。机器人通过语言模型协商动作并生成计划，在训练早期为策略学习提供指导；训练过程中，系统会在强化学习与语言协商之间动态切换。作者在仿真和实体机器人上使用本地及远程语言模型进行评估，并报告相较标准多智能体强化学习，该方法在早期训练中表现更好，对最终性能影响有限。

sections.text:
Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robot manipulation, but their deployment can remain unreliable due to spurious visual reliance and stochastic action generation, leading to grounding failures and kinematically unstable behaviors.

We introduce Selected Diffusion Noise (SDN), a training-free method that treats diffusion noise as a controllable degree of freedom for improving test-time reliability.

SDN samples multiple candidate action chunks and applies two-stage selection: it first filters candidates based on task-relevant visual grounding using a counterfactual negative set, then selects the kinematically most stable chunk based on JerkRMS.

Experiments on three VLA policies across both simulation and real-world environments show improvements of 8-10% and 18.33%, respectively, demonstrating SDN's effectiveness for test-time improvement.

summary.en: The paper introduces Selected Diffusion Noise (SDN), a training-free test-time method that treats diffusion noise as a controllable factor for improving VLA policy reliability. It samples candidate action chunks, filters them using task-relevant visual grounding and a counterfactual negative set, then selects the most kinematically stable chunk using JerkRMS. The authors report improvements across three policies in simulation and real-world environments, with gains stated as 8–10% and 18.33%, respectively.

sections.text:
Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place.

Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data.

However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data or lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. We investigate this question through controlled simulation experiments that vary robot and object masses.

We find that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object. Heavier robots require more demonstrations to attain the same performance as lighter robots.

Finally, because new hardware is rarely an option, we explore ways to lower an existing arm's inertia at contact with existing hardware, either by choosing a lower-inertia workspace before collecting data or by steering the demonstrator toward lower-inertia configurations during the task.

In both cases, the lower-inertia demonstrations are imitated more reliably. Project website: https://younghyopark.me/inertia-mismatch/

summary.en: The paper uses controlled simulation experiments to study how robot-object mass differences affect policy learning. The authors report that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning produces more reliable policies when a lighter robot handles a heavier object. Heavier robots require more demonstrations to match lighter robots' performance. The study also explores reducing contact inertia with existing hardware by selecting a lower-inertia workspace or guiding demonstrators toward lower-inertia configurations; demonstrations from both approaches are imitated more reliably.
summary.zh: 论文通过受控仿真实验研究机器人与物体质量差异对策略学习的影响。作者报告，强化学习在较广泛的质量组合下均能成功；行为克隆在轻型机器人操作较重物体时学到的策略更可靠。较重机器人需要更多示范，才能达到轻型机器人的同等表现。研究还探索利用现有硬件降低接触时惯性：采集数据前选择低惯性工作空间，或引导示范者采用低惯性构型；两种情况下，低惯性示范都更容易被模仿。

Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging.

Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction.

First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences.

Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy.

Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference.

On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets.

Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing

summary.en: The paper presents SimForcing, a framework for learning real-domain robot world models using simulation motion supervision. It transfers motion knowledge through latent-motion distillation and uses multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout, reducing dependence on prediction accuracy. The jointly trained student generates simulation conditions and real-domain videos without an additional world model at inference. The authors report the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among compared methods on Bridge, without external embodied pretraining; evaluation on InternData-A1 supports cross-dataset applicability. Initializing a VLA model with the world model also improved LIBERO success.

sections.text:
Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop.

We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model.

Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv.

Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.

summary.en: The paper introduces PDRVLA, a model that extracts physical-dynamics tokens from vision-language features to condition robot action generation without generating future videos online. Its lightweight module learns by predicting future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision from a frozen pretrained video world model. Training uses publicly available data expanded through human-to-robot synthesis and annotations. Across four simulation benchmarks, the reported success rates are 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations assess several supervision and conditioning choices.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions.

However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability.

To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself.

Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline.

These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions.

Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

summary.en: The paper proposes A³-VLA, which derives task-specific visual guidance from changes observed during manipulation. It generates candidate regions for target objects and the robot, then refines them offline with a visual segmentation model. An attention-allocation loss encourages language or robot-state tokens to focus on task-critical regions, while a contrastive loss aligns target-region representations with instructions and separates them from irrelevant regions. The authors report improvements across multiple VLA backbones on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, with average success-rate gains of 6.5% to 25.2% across benchmarks.

sections.text:
An ordered sequence of end-effector poses can give a redundant robot arm multiple valid joint configurations at each waypoint. Inverse kinematics (IK) computes these configurations. Choosing a configuration only for the next waypoint can leave the arm poorly placed for later waypoints. This may increase planned motion time or cause a later planning failure.

This paper presents Future-Window Inverse Kinematics (FWIK), an online method that selects IK solutions by considering a small window of future waypoints. FWIK generates several IK candidates, connects them in a layered joint-space graph, and ranks candidate paths with a simple motion-time estimate.

A learned model removes paths whose transitions are likely to cause self-collision. A standard MoveIt 2 planner then checks the next-waypoint IK goals from the remaining paths in ranked order, and the first goal that yields a valid trajectory is selected for execution.

We evaluate FWIK in simulation on two 7-DoF manipulators, the Franka Emika Panda and the KUKA LBR iiwa. Each method-planner setting contains five repetitions of 100 sequences with 50 waypoints.

Across Pilz, RRT-Connect, CHOMP, and STOMP, FWIK completes 96.8-100% of sequences and gives the shortest planned trajectory duration in all eight robot-planner settings. Its mean duration is 12.8-13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5-25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5-37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK.

The results show that a small future window can improve sequence completion and reduce planned motion time while leaving final trajectory validation to the motion planner.

summary.en: The paper presents FWIK, an online method for choosing inverse-kinematics solutions across a sequence of waypoints. It builds a layered graph of candidate joint configurations over a short future window, ranks paths by estimated motion time, and uses a learned model to remove transitions likely to cause self-collision. A MoveIt 2 planner then validates next-waypoint goals in rank order. In simulation with two seven-degree-of-freedom manipulators and four planners, the authors report 96.8–100% sequence completion and the shortest planned duration across eight settings.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向多航点逆运动学选择的在线方法 FWIK：为未来若干航点生成关节配置候选，在分层图中按运动时间估计排序，并用学习模型剔除可能自碰撞的路径；随后由 MoveIt 2 规划器依序验证下一航点目标。仿真涵盖两种七自由度机械臂及四种规划器。作者报告，八种机器人与规划器设置下序列完成率为 96.8%–100%，规划轨迹时长均为最短，且低于所比较的方法；最终轨迹仍由规划器验证。

sections.text:
Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models offer semantic and spatial priors for robot manipulation, but their parallel-gripper interfaces leave multi-finger contact coordination implicit. Adapting these models requires both timely grasp transitions and embodiment-specific hand trajectories.

We introduce InDex, an intent-conditioned framework that connects these two requirements. A normalized aperture signal, derived from retargeted demonstrations, supervises a scalar grasp intent while preserving full hand-action supervision.

Stage 1 learns synchronized end-effector-intent chunks; Stage 2 conditions a diffusion hand decoder on these predictions, visual-language context, and proprioception. Sequential optimization establishes the upstream interface before learning dexterous control with low-rate co-adaptation.

Across four simulated tasks, InDex with $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves 85.8% mean task success, improving the native policy by 35.5 percentage points, and reaches 69.0% on held-out objects with similar geometry without fine-tuning or recalibration.

Improvements also hold across three VLA backbones and separately trained real-world policies, where mean success increases from 71.0% to 83.0%.Component ablations and timing interventions support the value of explicit grasp-intent conditioning and expressive hand generation.

These results identify arm-hand coordination as an actionable bottleneck in adapting parallel-gripper priors to dexterous manipulation.

summary.en: The paper introduces InDex, an intent-conditioned framework for adapting vision-language-action models to dexterous manipulation. It supervises a scalar grasp intent from retargeted demonstrations while retaining full hand-action supervision. Stage 1 learns synchronized end-effector and intent chunks; Stage 2 trains a diffusion hand decoder conditioned on those predictions, visual-language context, and proprioception. In four simulated tasks, the authors report 85.8% mean success with π0.5, 35.5 percentage points above the native policy, and 69.0% on geometrically similar held-out objects without fine-tuning or recalibration. Improvements are also reported across three backbones and separately trained real-world policies.

sections.text:
Moving robot swarms from simulation into the physical world can be difficult because small discrepancies in hardware, timing and communication can cascade across interacting robots and alter group behaviour. This challenge is known as the reality gap.

When swarms operate in human environments, a second challenge emerges: a perceptual gap between what the swarm physically does and what human onlookers actually perceive. This study examines the same decentralised coordination code deployed across three robotic swarms-tabletop, aerial and human-scale mobile manipulators-during live artistic performances.

We find that while the underlying algorithms executed reliably on all three platforms, physical embodiment drastically altered visible motion-distorting execution timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaping trajectory geometry.

More importantly, audience surveys revealed that human interpretation does not mirror technical success: how observers attribute meaning (perceived purpose) and how they react emotionally (comfort versus threat) depend heavily on physical form. Meaning attribution and emotional responses did not vary together.

Our results demonstrate that successfully transferring swarm software to physical hardware is insufficient for real-world deployment. Addressing the reality gap does not guarantee that the resulting collective motion will be readily interpreted by human observers.

Swarms destined for human environments must be engineered not only for decentralised stability but also for the expressive physical dynamics through which humans interpret collective motion.

summary.en: The study examines reality and perceptual gaps by deploying the same decentralized coordination code on tabletop, aerial, and human-scale mobile-manipulator swarms in live artistic performances. The authors report reliable algorithm execution on all three platforms, while physical embodiment changed visible motion timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaped trajectories. Audience surveys found that perceived purpose and emotional responses such as comfort or threat depended on physical form and did not vary together. The authors argue that successful software transfer alone does not ensure interpretable motion.

sections.text:
Scaling real-world dexterous-grasp data collection is limited by the sustained human effort required to operate the robot, verify grasp outcomes, and reset objects between trials. Simulation can generate grasp candidates at scale, but their success on hardware remains uncertain.

We present AutoDex, a system that collects real-world dexterous-grasp data without continuous human operation. Given generated grasp candidates, AutoDex plans and executes grasps, labels their outcomes, and resets the object to continue collection across stable poses.

Multi-view object tracking supports labeling under hand-object occlusion, while residual-torque collision monitoring and pose-directed reset enable the loop to operate without continuous human supervision.

Using AutoDex, we collect over 3,500 grasp trials across 100 objects with Allegro and Inspire hands, recording both successes and failures together with synchronized visual observations and robot states.

AutoDex reduces human effort by more than an order of magnitude, requiring an estimated 0.2 human-hours to collect 500 trajectories compared with 9.3 for teleoperation. As AutoDex collects trials, it builds a library of physically validated grasps for subsequent execution.

In new object placements and obstacle configurations, retrieval from this library achieves 76% success, compared with 34% for candidates screened only in simulation. Code and data are available at https://snuvclab.github.io/AutoDex/.

summary.en: AutoDex automates real-world dexterous-grasp data collection by planning and executing generated grasp candidates, labeling outcomes, and resetting objects for further trials. Multi-view tracking, residual-torque collision monitoring, and pose-directed resets support operation without continuous human supervision. The system collected over 3,500 trials across 100 objects using Allegro and Inspire hands, recording successes, failures, observations, and robot states. The authors estimate 0.2 human-hours for 500 trajectories versus 9.3 hours for teleoperation. In new placements and obstacle configurations, library retrieval achieved 76% success, compared with 34% for simulation-screened candidates.

sections.text:
Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant.

Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions.

This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations.

Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives.

Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/

summary.en: ELA is an end-to-end framework for learning robot policies from video demonstrations, addressing the scarcity of action-labeled data. It jointly trains a latent action model, policy, and decoder so latent actions support both policy learning and decoding into continuous robot actions, alongside a handful of labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show consistent improvement over prior latent-action baselines. The authors also report that ELA can integrate with existing imitation-learning methods through lightweight, 4-million-parameter action decoders, without changing policy architectures or training objectives.
summary.zh: ELA 是一种从视频演示学习机器人策略的端到端框架，针对视频缺少动作标签而动作标注数据稀缺的问题。它联合训练潜在动作模型、潜在动作策略和动作解码器，使潜在动作同时服务于策略学习与连续机器人动作解码，并结合少量带动作标签的机器人演示。论文报告，在仿真和真实操作任务中，ELA 持续优于先前潜在动作基线。作者还称，该方法可通过轻量的400万参数动作解码器接入现有模仿学习方法，无需更改策略架构或训练目标。

Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive.

Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets.

We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization.

MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail.

To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization.

We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress.

MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.

Its five suites measure in-distribution performance and four generalization axes: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition. The authors introduce MESA-Gen, a task and demonstration generation pipeline built by improving MimicGen, and instantiate single-arm MESA and bimanual BiMESA on two platforms. Evaluations of seven baseline methods found that the strongest model scored 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA. The authors report broad consistency with RoboArena rankings; these findings reflect the benchmark evaluations described.

A central challenge in assistive brain-to-robot control is decoding a user's latent intent from complex and noisy brain signals. Prior approaches evaluate decoders as single-trial classifiers with accuracy-based metrics, but this neglects the inherently sequential nature of assistive control.

Since a planner must integrate intermittent, noisy decoder outputs over time, single-step accuracy can only be a proxy when predicting downstream task performance.

We formalize brain-to-robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), and prove that there is a sharp phase transition: regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon as long as pairs of goals are all decoder-distinguishable, but grows linearly otherwise.

We show that a single channel statistic, the worst-pair Chernoff information $\Gamma_{\min}$ sets this boundary. Then, we derive a closed-form regret predictor $U_{\mathrm{id}}(C)$, that can be computed from any confusion matrix in $O(K^2)$ time.

Across two domains spanning orthogonal information channels, we show that $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy can explain.

We then highlight a pathological accuracy trap, in which two decoders have identical validation accuracy 35.1% on real EEG data (BNCI2014001 subject 5) but result in a difference of $9.6\times$ in held-out regret, which $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts. Same-signal control confirms $U_{\mathrm{id}}$'s advantage with decoders that span independent feature channels.

Ultimately, our work provides a drop-in diagnostic to evaluate and select sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control.

summary.en: The paper models brain-to-robot assistive control as a partially observable Markov decision process. It claims regret remains uniformly bounded over the horizon when every pair of goals is decoder-distinguishable, and otherwise grows linearly. The authors identify worst-pair Chernoff information as the boundary statistic and derive a closed-form regret predictor from confusion matrices. Results across two domains suggest it explains cumulative planning regret beyond accuracy. On real EEG data, equal-accuracy decoders show a 9.6-fold difference in held-out regret; same-signal control supports the predictor’s advantage.

LLM-based robotic agent systems can generate programs for robot control, yet their generalization to new tasks often depends on elaborate scaffolding. Expanding their skill repertoires alone offers limited guidance on how to assess new capabilities or identify what remains beyond their reach.

We introduce META-Robot, a framework that couples self cognition with capability scaling by expanding the criteria through which an agent evaluates and develops its skills. At its core, action-level predicates make execution outcomes explicit and available for LLM reasoning.

The agent uses these assessments to identify its own limitations, extend relevant evaluation criteria, and guide the structured expansion of its skills. Proprioceptive feedback further grounds this process in the robot's physical state, enriching the evidence available for self-cognition.

Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate stronger overall task performance, generalization to new tasks, continued expansion of skills and evaluation criteria, and effective use of non-visual proprioceptive signals.

summary.en: The paper introduces META-Robot, a framework combining self-cognition with capability scaling in robotic agents. Action-level predicates make execution outcomes explicit for LLM reasoning. The agent uses these assessments to identify limitations, extend evaluation criteria, and guide structured skill growth, while proprioceptive feedback grounds the process in the robot’s physical state. Experiments in simulation and on real robots are reported to show stronger overall task performance and generalization to new tasks, continued expansion of skills and criteria, and effective use of non-visual proprioceptive signals.

For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, recent advances in agentic coding systems have potential to combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies.

We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation. Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications.

Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL).

GaP generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput.

Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines. Details, code, and data: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

summary.en: The paper focuses on Variational Automation tasks, where object geometry and pose vary more than in fixed automation, and introduces GaP, a multi-agent coding harness. Using a modular open robot skill library, it generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes. An internal simulation environment rehearses task instances with different graphs in parallel, allowing iterative refinement of graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput. Evaluation on eight new benchmarks, split between simulation and real-world tasks, suggests GaP achieves success rates significantly above baselines.

sections.text:
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering.

We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction.

To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels.

The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets.

Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.

It proposes Time-to-Goal (T2G), which learns temporal distances from latent-state triples in offline trajectories using a margin ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels. T2G replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast, and across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, average planning success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, approaching or surpassing hierarchical baselines.

sections.text:
Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs).

Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion.

In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms.

We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties.

Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution.

Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

summary.en: The paper proposes H²MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for humanoid control. It factors whole-body policies at the joint-degree-of-freedom level, conditioning each torque-actuated joint on descriptors of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. A closed-loop co-optimization mechanism jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories. Experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym show improved locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality compared with homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

sections.text:
Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization.

We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

summary.en: The paper introduces OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. It augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion, allowing agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark covers invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. The authors also develop a multimodal reinforcement-learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments report that this policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines.
